name: Persian written in Latin letters (Pinglish)
variety: Standard Iranian Persian (Tehran) written informally in Latin letters (Pinglish, Fingilish). The sounds are those of the fa profile; only the spelling differs, and because chat writing is colloquial, the colloquial Tehran forms noted below are frequent.
sources: Majidi, Mohammad-Reza and Ternes, Elmar (1999). Persian (Farsi). In Handbook of the International Phonetic Association. Cambridge University Press (first published in Journal of the International Phonetic Association 21(2), 1991).
Windfuhr, Gernot L. (1979). Persian Grammar: History and State of its Study. The Hague: Mouton.
Windfuhr, Gernot and Perry, John R. (2009). Persian and Tajik. In Windfuhr (ed.), The Iranian Languages. London: Routledge.
Lazard, Gilbert (1992). A Grammar of Contemporary Persian. Costa Mesa: Mazda Publishers.
Samareh, Yadollah (1977). The Arrangement of Segmental Phonemes in Farsi. Tehran University Press.
Mahootian, Shahrzad (1997). Persian. London: Routledge (Descriptive Grammars).
Ferguson, Charles A. (1957). Word stress in Persian. Language 33(2).
Kahnemuyipour, Arsalan (2003). Syntactic categories and Persian stress. Natural Language and Linguistic Theory 21(2).
Toosarvandani, Maziar (2004). Vowel length in Modern Farsi. Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 14(3).
Bijankhan, Mahmood and Nourbakhsh, Mandana (2009). Voice onset time in Persian initial and intervocalic stop production. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 39(3).

contrasts: six vowel qualities in two sets: the historically long, stable vowels /iː ɒː uː/ and the historically short, unstable vowels /e æ o/; in Tehran speech the sets differ mainly in quality, length is secondary
voiced versus voiceless obstruents; the voiceless stops and /tʃ/ are aspirated
one uvular phoneme /ɢ/ for the letters ق and غ, written gh or q in Latin letters
glottal stop /ʔ/ as a consonant in careful speech, written with an apostrophe or left out in Latin letters
single versus geminate consonants in careful speech, mainly in Arabic loans
/æ/ versus /ɒː/: the usual Latin spelling writes both as a, so this contrast is often not shown (some writers use aa or â for /ɒː/)
allophony: /ɢ/ is a voiced uvular stop [ɢ] word-initially, after a nasal and when geminate; a voiced fricative [ɣ] or [ʁ] between vowels and in unstressed syllable onsets; devoiced toward [q] or [χ] before voiceless consonants and often word-finally
/k ɡ/ are palatalised to [c ɟ] before the front vowels /iː e æ/ and in syllable-final position, velar before back vowels

/p t k tʃ/ are aspirated, most strongly word-initially and before a stressed vowel; voiced stops are short-lag or prevoiced word-initially and fully voiced between vowels (Bijankhan and Nourbakhsh 2009)
/t d/ are denti-alveolar; /l/ is always clear
/n/ is [ŋ] before velars and uvulars and [m] before labials
/ɾ/ is a tap between vowels, a trill when geminate and often word-initially, and may be devoiced or fricated word-finally
/ʔ/ and /h/ in coda position are weakened or dropped in colloquial speech with lengthening of the vowel ([bæʔd] 'after' becomes [bæːd])
a vowel-initial word begins with a glottal stop or glottalised onset
/e æ o/ are clearly short only in non-final open syllables; in closed and in final syllables they approach the duration of /iː ɒː uː/
colloquial /ɒːn/ and /ɒːm/ are raised to [un] and [um]; Pinglish usually writes the colloquial form (nemidoonam for written nemidɒːnæm)
syllable_structure: CV, CVC, CVCC; every syllable has an onset (a glottal stop fills an empty one)
phonotactics: no onset clusters: initial clusters of loanwords are broken up by a vowel
coda clusters of two consonants are frequent (dust, fekɾ)
vowel hiatus is filled by [j], [ʔ] or [w]
geminates occur between vowels and word-finally, mostly in Arabic loans, and are often simplified colloquially
Latin spelling writes the short vowels and usually the ezafe (ketabe man), which the Persian script leaves out

common Latin spellings: kh = /x/, gh or q = /ɢ/, sh = /ʃ/, ch = /tʃ/, zh = /ʒ/, j = /dʒ/, oo or u = /uː/, ee or i = /iː/, a or aa = /æ/ or /ɒː/, ei or ey = /ej/, ow or ou = /ow/; there is no fixed standard

stress.type: fixed by word class, mostly word-final; realised as a pitch accent
stress.rule: Nouns, adjectives and most adverbs are stressed on the last syllable, including derivational suffixes and the plural -hɒː; enclitics (ezafe -e, indefinite -i, object marker -ɾɒː, pronominal and copula clitics, -o 'and') are unstressed; in verbs the prefixes mi- and be- take the stress and the negative prefix næ-/ne- takes it from them; unprefixed past forms stress the last syllable of the stem, before the personal ending; vocatives have initial stress.
stress.cues: mainly pitch: a rise to a high peak on the stressed syllable; duration and intensity are weak cues (Abolhasanizadeh, Bijankhan and Gussenhoven 2012)

rhythm.vowel_reduction: weak: /e æ o/ are shortened and somewhat centralised in unstressed open syllables but keep their category; no schwa
rhythm.notes: Syllable-timed is the usual label in the descriptive literature. No published nPVI value is cited here.

length.notes: As in the fa profile: vowel length is not contrastive on its own; /iː ɒː uː/ are inherently longer than /e æ o/, most clearly in open syllables (Toosarvandani 2004). Doubled vowel letters in Latin spelling (aa, oo, ee) mark vowel quality, not length. Geminates are contrastive in careful speech only.

intonation.declarative: each accentual phrase (a content word with its clitics) has a rising accent that peaks on the stressed, usually final, syllable; the last accented phrase, normally the word before the verb, carries the nuclear accent, and the pitch then falls to a low boundary with the verb deaccented
intonation.yes_no_question: same word order as the statement; higher register and wider range, lengthening of the final syllable, and a high boundary tone giving a final rise
intonation.wh_question: nuclear accent on the question word, the rest of the sentence deaccented, low final boundary
intonation.continuation: high boundary tone at the end of a non-final phrase or clause
intonation.accent_shape: L+H*: low at the start of the accentual phrase rising to a peak on the stressed syllable; H* in monosyllables and initially stressed words
intonation.notes: Analysis of Sadat-Tehrani (2007, 2009, 2011) and Mahjani (2003). Material after the focus is deaccented.

phonation: the glottal stop is often realised as creaky voice on the neighbouring vowels

problems: Latin a is always /æ/ unless it is written aa or followed by an apostrophe, so /ɒː/ is lost in the usual spelling (khoda gives [xoda], madar [madar], iran [iran])
an apostrophe after a is read as the mark of /ɒː/, so the common use of the apostrophe for the glottal stop gives the wrong vowel and no [ʔ] (ba'd gives [bɑd])
word stress follows the default penultimate rule ([sˈalɑm], [kˈetab], [xˈahar], [mˈadar]) instead of final stress, and prefixed verbs are not stressed on the prefix
gh and q give q1 as in fa: the voiceless uvular stop of the base table followed by an undefined '1'; no [ɢ] or [ɣ]
zh is read as [z] plus [h] (only jh gives [ʒ]), x is read as [ks] although it is a common spelling of /x/, and ei is read as two vowels [e.i] instead of the diphthong [ej] (kheili gives [xeˈili])
the word list fa_list is in Persian script, so Latin-letter words are read by letter rules only
/k ɡ/ have no palatalised variants, ر is always a trill, and /n/ does not become [ŋ] before velars, as in fa
good: the digraphs kh, sh, ch, gh, oo, ou, ee and aa are read as single sounds
uses the fa phoneme table, so vowel and consonant qualities match the Persian-script voice

notes: Same sound system as fa. Latin spelling is unstandardised and writes colloquial Tehran forms, so a reader must accept several spellings for one sound and cannot tell /æ/ from /ɒː/ without a lexicon.
